author: Natalie Armendariz
title: The You You Think You Know
body: To be fair, I wasn’t exactly making it difficult for them to assume. I wore baggy clothes, kept my hair short and spiky, went to raves I had absolutely no business being at, and spent the rest of my time attempting to skate, breakdance, and tag up walls in the dark. It was a strangely formative combination of things, though I wouldn’t realize just how much they shaped me until later.

I was a “tomboy” in every possible sense of the word. At one point, I decided Natalie didn’t really suit me and started going by Nate. It wasn’t casual, either, even if it was short-lived. I started signing my schoolwork that way until a teacher informed me that, no, I couldn’t simply rename myself on assignments.

But you know what? I liked Nate. It felt right for me then, and there was nothing particularly complicated about it. I wasn’t trying to find myself or make a statement. I was just being a kid, before it occurred to me to wonder how I made sense to anyone else.

As I got older, I tried harder to fit in, though I never really quite mastered it. I somehow went from breakdancing with my brother’s friends to hanging out with cheerleaders, only to find the funny, offbeat ones who didn’t quite fit the stereotype. Even when I was trying to belong, I seemed to find my way to the edges.

There’s a point as you get older when being yourself stops being entirely instinctive. Suddenly, there’s an awareness of how you’re perceived, where you fit, and which parts of yourself people seem to respond to. Without really meaning to, you start noticing what earns approval and learning how to read a room.

author: John Zacharias
title: The Difference Between Privacy and Secrecy
body: I had arrived early for dinner. He was still changing, his wife was attempting to rescue a sauce, and I had been left in the hallway with a glass of wine and the considerable responsibility of staying out of the way. One door stood half open. My friend emerged from the room, pulled it shut behind him, and said, almost automatically, “Sorry, absolute chaos in there.”

Modern culture encourages disclosure with almost religious enthusiasm. Couples are urged to share everything. Friends are expected to be available. Public figures are regarded as evasive when they decline personal questions. Phones contain locations, correspondence, photographs, medical information, purchases, private jokes, unfinished thoughts, and enough incidental evidence to support several competing biographies. The possibility of knowing more about someone is constantly present, and possibility has a habit of disguising itself as entitlement.

Privacy gives a person somewhere to remain a person without an audience. A private journal, an hour alone, a conversation with a doctor, an old letter kept in a drawer, a friendship whose every detail is not reported to a partner: these preserve an interior life. Healthy relationships require some version of this interiority because closeness between two whole people is far more interesting than closeness achieved by dismantling both of them for inspection.

Consider money. You may reasonably regard the exact amount you spent on a birthday present as private. A large undisclosed debt in a marriage with shared finances belongs to another category. A private lunch with an old friend need not produce minutes for household review. An affair concealed from a partner concerns the partner rather directly. You are entitled to have thoughts you have not yet articulated. You become less entitled to hide facts that another person needs in order to make meaningful decisions about their own life.

author: Devina
title: Every person you meet carries a different version of you in their mind
body: Sometimes, we wonder how others perceive us. Perhaps we all want to be seen as nice, kind, or any other words associated with positive traits. And to be perceived the way we want, we often become extremely careful about how we carry ourselves in society.
We measure every interaction. We curate the stories we choose to tell so we won’t be labeled “too much” and we restrain ourselves from doing something silly because we fear being seen as weird.

Someone might think you are shy simply because you are the quietest person in the room. But maybe you are dealing with personal struggles and still choosing to show up, while all you are really doing is being observant.
However, there are also people who are inspired by your hard work and touched by your kindness. Then, they tell you how much your existence matters in their lives.
